summary:
Allwork.Space reports that Hong Kong is drawing professionals back after the 2019 unrest and strict COVID restrictions triggered an exodus, driven by a booming IPO market and the city's revival as a global financial hub. Total funds raised, including IPOs, rose 76% year-on-year to about $83.5 billion in the first eight months of 2026, and Hong Kong overtook Switzerland as the top cross-border wealth hub.

Executive search firms report finance professionals returning from Singapore, London, Dubai and mainland China. Lee Brantingham of H.I.E.C. says inquiries and relocation activity have rebounded strongly since the 2023 low, with asset management, private wealth and family offices as the cornerstone and fastest growth in AI integration, compliance and risk management roles.

InvestHK reports more than 400 companies set up or expanded local entities in the first half of 2026, up 9%, expected to bring over HK$53 billion ($6.8 billion) in FDI and create over 8,600 jobs.

Office demand is recovering. Savills reports Grade A Central office rents up 4.8% quarter-on-quarter in Q2 with vacancy falling from 10.2% to 9.4%; Jack Tong notes hedge funds and quantitative funds pre-leasing large contiguous floor plates. Knight Frank reports Central premium vacancy falling to 9.7% in July from 14.5% at the start of the year. Susquehanna International Group plans to triple its Hong Kong office space.

Hong Kong is also passing a bill extending tax incentives to more fund firms. Economic growth hit 5.9% in Q1 2026, aided by AI-related demand and cross-border financial activity.

Structural caveats remain: the 2020 national security law, high property prices and cost of living. Returnees like teacher Emily Hampson-Ford cite savings potential and lifestyle. Brantingham frames the trend as structural evolution toward a more China-integrated international hub, not a cyclical recovery.
